chunks: Muhammad ibn Ya'qub from Muhammad ibn Yahya from Ahmad ibn Muhammad from al-Husayn ibn Sa'id from al-Qasim ibn Muhammad from Ali ibn Abi Hamzah from Abu Basir from one of them (peace be upon them both) who said:

I asked him: Does one Adhan suffice? He said: 'If you pray in congregation, only one Adhan and one Iqamah suffice. And if you are alone and hastening to a matter you fear might be missed, the Iqamah suffices for you, except for Fajr and Maghrib, for it is appropriate that you give the Adhan in them and give the Iqamah, because they are not shortened in them as you shorten in the other prayers.'

Al-Sheikh (may Allah have mercy on him) said: And there is no harm if a person, when praying alone without an Imam, restricts himself to the Iqamah and leaves the Adhan in three prayers: Dhuhr, Asr, and the last 'Isha. And he does not leave the Adhan and Iqamah in Maghrib and Fajr, because they are two prayers that are not shortened in travel. The mention of that has passed in the two preceding hadiths, and what is narrated adds emphasis to it:

key_terms.أَذَانٌ: Adhan: The call to prayer announcing the time for salat.
key_terms.إِقَامَةٌ: Iqamah: The second call to prayer immediately preceding the start of salat.
key_terms.تُقْصِرُ: Tuqsir: To shorten (prayers), specifically referring to the reduction of rak'ahs during travel.

ai.seo_question: What are the rules for Adhan and Iqamah when praying alone in Shia jurisprudence?
ai.summary: Shaykh al-Tusi clarifies that while the Fajr and Maghrib prayers require both Adhan and Iqamah even for the solitary worshiper due to their fixed duration (not being shortened like other prayers), he permits omitting the Adhan for Dhuhr, Asr, and the final Isha in favor of brevity. This ruling highlights the Shia jurisprudential emphasis on practical ease (rukhas) while maintaining the distinct ritual identity of the two prayers that do not undergo qasr. The distinction underscores the theological link between prayer length and the legal status of travel, reinforcing the sanctity of the morning and evening prayers.
